# COMP110 Data Analysis Project

## Idea
I analyzed whether programming assignments improve student understanding of course material.

## Analysis

### Programming Effectiveness vs Understanding

![Graph 1]({{ site.baseurl }}/image.png)

This boxplot shows how understanding changes across programming effectiveness ratings. It is easier to interpret than a scatterplot because it summarizes the spread of understanding scores for each programming effectiveness rating.

### Difficulty vs Understanding

![Graph 2]({{ site.baseurl }}/image-1.png)

This graph suggests that as difficulty increases, understanding may decrease slightly, however the results are retty scattered. This could indicate that students who find the course more difficult struggle more with understanding the material, but also that at that point people still understood the content well.

### Distribution of Programing Effectiveness

![Graph 3]({{ site.baseurl }}/image-2.png)

This distribution shows how students generally perceive programming assignments. Most of the responses are on the higher end, indicating that students find them useful overall.

## Conclusion

My analysis suggests that programming assignments are generally effective in helping students understand course material. The boxplot comparing programming effectiveness and understanding shows that as students rate programming assignments as more effective, their reported understanding tends to increase. This indicates a positive relationship between practice-based work and learning outcomes.

However, the data is not perfectly consistent, as there is still a wide range of understanding levels at each effectiveness rating. This suggests that while programming assignments are helpful, they are not the only factor influencing student understanding. Other factors such as prior experience, study habits, or lecture clarity may also play a role.

Based on these findings, I recommend incorporating more optional practice problems both during and outside of class. This could help reinforce learning without overwhelming students with required work. A useful extension of this idea would be to track how often students complete optional practice and compare that with their understanding levels.

One potential trade-off is that adding more practice problems could increase student workload and stress, especially if they are required. To balance this, practice problems could remain optional and be auto-graded so that students who choose to do them can, and those that choose not to won't.

Overall, the data supports the idea that practice problems is valuable, but future improvements should consider balancing effectiveness with workload and exploring additional factors that impact student understanding.

## Future work

Future analysis could track how often students complete optional practice problems and how that affects understanding.
